content: Chasteberry (Vitex agnus-castus) is used for various indications, and its dosing depends on the specific condition being treated. For premenstrual syndrome (PMS), the recommended dose is 4–20 mg per day. For premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), the dose is 20–40 mg per day. The maximum daily dose should not exceed 1800 mg. Other conditions for which chasteberry is used include acne, benign prostatic hyperplasia, fibrocystic breast disease, female infertility, lactation issues, menopausal symptoms, menstrual irregularities, progesterone insufficiency, and impotence. Clinical evidence, such as a randomized controlled trial published in BMJ (2001;322:134-137), has demonstrated benefits of chasteberry compared to placebo for PMS. It is possibly effective for treating PMDD and PMS. Chasteberry may interact with certain medications by decreasing their effects through pharmacodynamic antagonism. These interactions are theoretical and of minor significance, with the clinical relevance being unknown. Medications potentially affected include antipsychotics such as aripiprazole, benperidol, chlorpromazine, clozapine, droperidol, fluphenazine, haloperidol, iloperidone, loxapine (including inhaled formulations), olanzapine, paliperidone, perphenazine, pimozide, prochlorperazine, promethazine, quetiapine, risperidone, thioridazine, thiothixene, trifluoperazine, ziprasidone, and zotepine. Adverse effects associated with chasteberry include acne, agitation, allergic reactions, alopecia, dry mouth, gastrointestinal upset, headache, intermenstrual bleeding, itching, changes in menstrual flow, nausea, rash, tachycardia, tiredness, and urticaria. Chasteberry is contraindicated in individuals with hormone-sensitive conditions such as breast cancer, endometriosis, ovarian cancer, uterine cancer, and uterine fibroids. It is also contraindicated during in vitro fertilization, pregnancy, and lactation due to safety concerns. It is classified as unsafe for use during pregnancy and lactation. In terms of pregnancy safety categories, chasteberry does not fall under Category A, which is generally considered safe based on controlled studies in pregnant women showing no evidence of fetal risk.
